title: Xserve introduction 2002
speaker: Steve Jobs
content:
Good morning.

I'm Steve Jobs and I'd like to thank you all for coming.

Um, we've got a really interesting morning plan, uh, because we're going to introduce our first real server.

And we wanted to take you through it.

We've got a few presentations, uh, I'm going to do an overview.

We got a presentation on the software and remote management.

Uh, we got a presentation on sales, support and service.

We got a few partners and customers and then we'll do a Q&A.

We had three hours down on the agenda.

I'm hoping we only take about two.

So, um, get you out of here a little after 11:00 and then we've got some stuff set up in the piano bar across the hall here where you can go get your hands on some of the stuff yourself.

So, let's get going.

This calendar year Apple has already introduced a stream of innovation.

Uh, just since January, we introduced uh, the new iMac, which has been a really big hit for us.

It's selling very well and I think it's one of the best products we've ever made.

We also introduced a um, desktop for our education customers, the eMac.

And this has been received very well by our customers.

We're in the first quarter of selling it and we expect to do very well this quarter.

The reaction so far also has been very strong from our education customers.

We also introduced an upgraded PowerBook that's got a dramatically better display on it and the industry's first DVI connector on a portable.

So you can connect to new projectors with DVI connectors on them, but also you can connect to our displays.

So this PowerBook can drive a Cinema HD display and has all the graphics and video memory inside it to be able to do that and so you can triple your pixels when you get that get to your desk and plug in one connector all digitally.

And last week, we introduced an amazing, or we previewed, excuse me, an amazing new product, Mac OS 10 Jaguar, the next release of Mac OS 10.

We had our most successful developer conference last year in the company's history, which is saying a lot given the travel and budget restrictions this year.

Uh, as you may know, the number of registered Apple developers has doubled in the last 12 months and all of the new developers are principally Unix and Java developers and we are so excited to have people coming to our developer conference that wouldn't even talk to us before our Unix based Mac OS 10.

Uh, Jaguar, which we previewed, which will be available late this summer, has a ton of new features in it.

Some major enhancements to mail, a whole new address book, Inkwell, which is probably the best handwriting recognition out there, uh, which came from, you know what?

Uh, and universal access so that we, we don't leave anybody behind.

Um, a new finder, something incredible called Quartz Extreme, which is taking our whole Quartz graphics pipeline and putting it through our graphics hardware so that it is uh, amazing what you can do now or what you will be able to do with Quartz Extreme.

A technology called Rendezvous, which allows multiple computers and devices, let's say in a home or in a business, to automatically find each other.

It's dynamic discovery over IP networks with zero configuration.

It's really, really cool and our developers loved it.

Uh, two of the biggest things we introduced was, was QuickTime 6, which is a whole new version of QuickTime based on MPEG 4.

This is the best MPEG 4 streaming video solution around and it's going to be bundled in uh, the next release of Mac OS 10 coming out late this summer.

And instant messaging coming to the Mac, integrated right into the operating system, uh, in an application called iChat.

It's totally compatible with AOL's AIM instant messaging network.

And it's the first time AOL's sort of let another company into the tent officially.

And all of this stuff, of course, runs on Mac OS 10, which is Unix, true Unix under the hood.

And as a matter of fact, we are now the largest supplier of Unix in the world.

Isn't that incredible?

I'll say that again.

Apple is now the largest Unix supplier in the world.

It's hard to believe.

And uh, that's why all these Unix developers now are coming to Apple and Mac OS 10.

So that was Jaguar.

So we've seen, uh, already, we're, we're only in our fifth month.

We've seen a tremendous stream of innovation so far this year, continuing what we've done for the last 18 months to try to uh, innovate our way through this uh, this economic period.

So we're going to add another piece of innovation today coming from Apple, which is a server and we call it Xserve.

Uh, Xserve is a new server from Apple.

Now, when you think about servers, you think about the enterprise, right?

And when you think about the enterprise and Apple, you're more likely to think about this than than anything else.

But it's not really true.

Uh, though, though we are not on every desktop in every Fortune 500 corporation, we are in most Fortune 500 corporations.

And uh, they have departments that use Macs.

Uh, AOL Time Warner uses a lot of Macs.

Their magazines every week are put out on Macs.

Uh, companies like Disney, companies like in biotech, like Genentech, uh, usually half or more of their computers are Macs.

So there are a lot of Macs in a lot of Fortune 500 corporations.

But uh, Xserve is really designed not only for business, but also for education because we have a large presence there as well.

So, if there's one word uh, that I would say describes our entrance into the server market, it is um, humble.

We know we have a lot to learn.

And uh, this is our first offering.

Uh, we've listened to our customers a lot and we think we got a pretty hot product, but we know that for everything we know, there's 10 things we don't know.

So we're approaching this uh, we're approaching this very humbly.

So Xserve, what is it?

It's a 1U server solution designed from the ground up.

It's been customer driven and our customers have told us they want to do the following things.

They want to do file and print service, obviously.

They want to do web and email service.

They want to um, do database on their server.

They want to do QuickTime streaming.

This is a way to, and they want to stream, you know, hundreds of streams.

Boom.

And uh, they want to do computational service.

Uh, as an example, our uh, customers in biotech want to run probably the most popular program in biotech, they run dozens of times a day called Blast.

And they want a uh, a computa, one or a cluster of servers to run this very fast.

So, what did they want to see in a server?

Well, the first thing they want from Apple is a dedicated server platform.

They don't want to use a uh, uh, a Power Mac G4 as a server.

They want a dedicated server platform.

Uh, they want it to be rack mounted.

It's the most efficient uh, way to do it.

That's how they do it now and they want to see that from Apple.

Uh, they want a lot of storage flexibility.

Some customers need a little storage, some customers need a lot of storage and they want the flexibility to design the storage that they need.

They want serviceability.

Uh, they know that these things uh, need to be very reliable, but sometimes do need to be serviced and they want great serviceability on this.

And of course, they have to be able to manage these things remotely.

So they want great remote management.

So we're, I'm going to go through all these things and tell you what we've done with Xserve.

To start with, Xserve is a dedicated server platform.

So let, let me take you through the architecture.

First, we start off with a 1 GHz G4 processor, which has 256k of internal level two cache running at the processor speed.

This is a very, very fast chip.

Um, faster than than most chips that chip in servers today.

And to this we add an external 2 megabyte cache, which is DDR SRAM.

Very, very fast cache for a gigabyte per second throughput to the processor.

So it's got a level two internal cache and a level three external cache.

To that, we add a mirror, a second processor with its own cache.

So we've got dual 1 GHz G4s, each with their own level two cache, each with a large level three cache.

Okay.

To that, we add a system controller.

Now, this system controller is a custom ASIC that we've done and it provides exceptional throughput.

Uh, way more than than than most of the other stuff on the market.

And it's got built in it, uh, gigabit Ethernet and it's got FireWire and as we'll see a whole bunch of other things built right in it in a single chip.

Next, we add onto that up to 2 gigabytes of DDR SRAM.

This is the first time DDR SD RAM, excuse me, has been used in a 1U server that we know of.

First time.

266 MHz double the rate of the memory in every other server that we've been able to find.

It's also the first Apple DDR SD RAM system that we will have shipped.

Then we add a PCI slot with a second gigabit Ethernet to it.

So this server is going to come standard with two gigabit Ethernet ports.

These are ports that are 10, 100 and gigabit Ethernet full auto detection.

Next, we add an IO channel out of the system controller and we add quad ATA 100 drives.

These are all on independent controllers, all have independent channels in through the system controller.

A CD ROM and two 64 bit 66 MHz PCI slots for expansion.

We also have three FireWire ports, two USB ports, a serial console port and all of those other kinds of things as well.

Now, this is going to be the first mainstream server to use ATA drives.

Most of the other ones use scuzzy drives.

We're going with ATA drives because it turns out they're just as fast as scuzzy drives now and they offer some real benefits in terms of larger capacities.

This is the fastest Mac architecture we've ever built.

Again, featuring dual GHz G4s, 266 MHz DDR SD RAM, quad independent ATA drives, dual gigabit Ethernet ports and two 64 bit 66 MHz PCI ports.

So this is a dedicated server platform, fastest architecture we've ever built.

Next, rack mounted.

This is Xserve.

This is what it looks like.

Let me show you actually, I've got one here.

Got a few here actually.

This is Xserve.

Here's five of them and here's one of them.

This is the back of the product.

This is the top.

Let me slide it out.

That's what it looks like.

We've got our four ATA 100 drives right there in the front.

We've got our CD ROM.

We've got fans right here.

Power supply.

Dual G4 processors.

2 gigabytes of DDR SD RAM and our three PCI slots.

One for the second gigabit Ethernet and two for expansion.

So that's what it looks like inside.

Now, you can put these in a rack of course and you can just start stacking them up in a rack.

And if you fill this rack, what you'll get is 84 processors, storage of up to 20 terabytes in a 42U rack.

So, rack mounted.

Yes.

Storage flexibility.

We are shipping with 60 gigabyte and 120 gigabyte ATA 100 drives.

Now, we support four drive bays and so if you put 120 gigabytes in each of those, you get 480 gigabytes in a 1U rack mount server.

So, up to 480 gigabytes online with quad ATA 100 drives, that's 400 megabytes per second throughput off the drives, which is huge.

It's also very important when you're doing file service, when you're doing QuickTime streaming, etcetera.

Your disk bandwidth is very, very important.

We've got striping and mirroring.

We've got smart drive monitoring.

We are actually monitoring these drives to look at their error rates, to look at their, their all the statistics about the drive so we can do predictive failure on them, which we'll talk about in a little bit.

And we've got a CD ROM built in for of course software install and restore.

These drives are hot pluggable.

We've designed a really nice carriage where you can unplug them.

And so just, you know, boom, boom, boom, boom.

Really easy.

Take one out.

Just that's it.

Very simple.

And they are hot pluggable.

That's it.

So, 480 gigabytes of storage, hot pluggable, four drives, I think we've delivered storage flexibility.

Next, serviceability.

You can service an Xserve in seconds.

Of course, you can service the drives like we just saw.

But in terms of the units themselves, they literally just slide out.

There's nothing extra to buy.

The rack mount guides are supplied as part of Xserve.

There's no top to take off.

So you can just literally slide the thing part of the way out or all the way out.

There's no nothing to take off to get at the guts and to service almost every component in seconds.

So, we also have hardware monitoring where we try to alert you to what needs service in some cases ahead of time.

So, what are we monitoring with hardware?

The drive status and pre fail, which is part of that smart disk technology.

We're monitoring the temperature of both the processor and the enclosure.

We're monitoring that the fans are working and what their RPMs are.

We're monitoring the power supply voltages and we're monitoring that the network connections are established.

And you will see more about this a little later.

It's really impressive what we can do with this.

We also have built in security since this is so easy to open up.

Uh, we have an enclosure security lock that keeps it from being opened.

We have an intrusion alert that lets you know if it's been opened and we have a software lock so that you can lock down FireWire, USB and the CD ROM from letting anyone in.

So we've tried to think of the type of security that people want in a modern day server.

So, this is Xserve.

You can service anything in seconds.

We think we've built in state of the art hardware monitoring and security and have a very strong serviceability story.

So pricing and availability.

Pricing on Xserve starts at $29.99.

There are two standard models.

One comes with one 1 GHz G4, the other comes with dual GHz G4 processors.

One quarter gigabyte of DDR memory, the other with a half a gigabyte of DDR memory.

Both come with 60 gig drives as standard.

One for $29.99, one for $39.99.

But most people aren't going to buy these standard configurations.

They're going to configure one exactly like they want.

You can go to our website and do that.

Select the server page, select one of our standard models or customize it any way you want.

Thousands and thousands of configurations.

Now, how does this compare to the competition?

What does it look like out there?

Well, we picked a few different things to compare to.

Here's Xserve.

We're going to take the dual processor model.

We're going to take our competitors and configure them as close as we can to Xserve.

So here's a Dell Power Edge 1650 with dual processors.

Uh, configured it's about $4277.

An IBM eServer X3300 for 5186.

And a Sun, this is the closest Sun we could get.

The low end Suns are not competitive and it's uh, it's almost $20,000.

So, three of these are 1U servers.

The Sun is a 4U server.

1U servers.

And uh, as I mentioned, they have dual processors in them, dual 1 GHz G4 in Xserve.

Uh, the other two, uh, the middle two use Pentium 3s.

They can't put a Pentium 4 in because they can't get the heat out in a 1U server.

So they use Pentium 3s at 1.4 GHz and the Sun uh, uses a dual 900 MHz Ultra Sparc 3s.

Now, if we look at level, they all have uh, level two caches built in.

If we look at level three caches though, which really can speed up performance, the Xserve again has 4 megabytes of level three cache, 2 megabytes on each processor.

Uh, and the Sun has 8 megabytes of level three cache, but the Dell and the IBM have no level three cache and it's not even possible to add it.

So this does affect performance.

In terms of memory, uh, we've loaded uh, the Dell and the IBM up to get to 512 megabytes.

The Sun, the lowest you can buy it with is 2 gigabytes, which is great.

Um, but if you notice, the Xserve is the only one that uses 266 MHz DDR memory.

The rest of them are at 133 MHz uh, SD RAM.

And that makes a difference in performance, double the bandwidth to memory.

On the disc drive front, uh, we've loaded them up to get as close as we can to Xserve with its 60 gigabytes.

We've got 73 gigabytes uh, on the middle two and about the same on the Sun.

If you notice again, everyone else uses scuzzy drives.

We think there is an absolute trend to ATA drives now that they've gotten as fast as scuzzy drives and uh, are less expensive and uh, larger capacity.

But if you look at the total capacity of each of these servers, we've got four bays in the Xserve for 480 gigabytes of storage.

But look at the two middle ones, 219 gigabytes max on the Dell with three bays and 144 gigabytes uh, on both the IBM and the Sun.

So all three of these servers have a lot less storage capacity than and flexibility than Xserve does.

Ethernet, uh, again, uh, uh, Xserve and Dell come standard with dual gigabit Ethernet.

We've loaded the IBM up.

Uh, you can't get dual gigabit Ethernet on the Sun, but we've, we've ordered the optional uh, single gigabit Ethernet included in that price.

So again, the prices for these things are um, as I've mentioned.

But these prices are um, for Linux on the middle two servers.

Mac OS 10 server on Xserve of course, Linux on the middle two and Solaris of course on the Sun.

But what if you want to run Windows on the middle two?

You can service it in seconds with intrusion alerts and hardware monitoring. And remote management. For remote management, I'm going to go uh back to our agenda here. We're going to go to the second topic on our agenda, the software and remote management. And I'm going to turn it over to Phil Schiller. But before I do, I forgot to do one thing, which I want to do, which is just uh pull one of these guys out so you can see how easy this is.

That's all there is to it. To get to every part in the server. So, take a look at one of these after the presentation and see for yourself how easy it is. Phil?

So now, thank you Phil.
Now we get to how are we going to service, support and sell these servers.
And you might think, wow, Apple's Apple's never done this before.
Apple doesn't do anything close to this before, but you might be wrong.
So here to tell us about that is Tim Cook.
Tim is our executive vice president who runs operations, sales and support and uh how are we going to service and support and sell these things, Tim?
Thank you Steve.
Good morning.
So I'd like to talk about both support and sales.
You've heard a lot about the product features and I'd like to first start by saying that we fully recognize that server support is really, really hard.
And so as Steve indicated earlier, we've entered into this very humbly.
We discovered two things as we began to look at this and why it's really, really hard.
And the first is that the applications running on servers are generally mission critical.
They're things that must happen.
So for me that might be taking orders, hopefully many of them, fulfilling orders, shipping orders, invoicing customers, things you can't stop.
Also, there's a fundamental lack of integration among most of the solutions on the market today.
And this has a this has a consequence that's really awful for customers, which is they have more issues and maybe even worse than that, when they have an issue, the timely response really isn't there.
So with that kind of backdrop, we went out and asked our customers, what do you want?
And when when we asked that, we got back seven simple kind of things.
Maybe not simple to deliver, but fairly simple to understand.
The very first was they really don't want support.
They want products to work.
Now this this is a fairly simple thing maybe to understand.
But so we looked at how do we provide this?
And as it turns out for those of you that are using Macs today, you may not know but but you've seen the results of, we have very robust quality assurance processes in Apple.
And it's because we control the whole of the solution.
Our reliability testing and engineering is enormous before we bring a product to market.
And maybe more importantly than both of those, our customers that are operating in mixed environments tell us that the Mac is better.
And that's the ultimate test.
The second thing they told us was that they want really expert technical support.
Really expert.
When they have a problem, they don't want to get on the phone with someone that's just been trained for three weeks.
Now this is not what they want.
And so we looked into see how do we shape up here?
Well, there was a survey done in consumer reports, very unbiased survey.
Grantedly, it's about consumers, but I think what it shows is the customer centric kind of culture in companies.

The next thing our customers told us was that they wanted problems solved, not a lot of finger pointing.
Well this industry that that I've been in for now almost 20 years and that most of you have have been customers in for a long time, I've seen more cartoons in this area than any other in anything other in our in our whole industry.
I could probably name the three guys and you could name them too, but what happens?
You call the hardware company and the hardware company, what do they say?
Go to the OS company.

What do they say?
Go to the hardware company.
And pretty soon you feel like the rat in the maze, bouncing up against the walls, never quite finding the way to the end of the maze.
Well at Apple, we're fundamentally different in this regard because we're delivering a solution.
It just so happens that this solution has software and hardware in it.
It's been designed as a solution to do something.
So we feel pretty good in this space as well.
The fourth thing they told us was they wanted access to us not 8 to 5, not the banker's hours, but every minute, every day all year long.
Well as it turns out, we do this today in Apple for some of our customers.
We have a select a group of customers that really demand this today.
So again, we have experience here.
The next thing they told us was they a group of them wanted to be self-sufficient.
Particularly in the hardware area.
So what have we done?
Look at this.
Steve showed this earlier.
Pull it out, replace.
Very simple, very fast.
You can do it in seconds.
I've been doing manufacturing a long time.
I've never seen anything this good before.
You can literally train someone with very limited knowledge to do this in seconds.
So we feel really good in this space as well.
Now a group of them said, well, yeah, that's fine, but I want on-site support.
I don't want to touch anything.
And so as you probably know, we also do this today for a group of our customers.
So again, we feel pretty good in this space.
The next thing they told us was that they wanted speed.
Really, really fast.
In fact, the group that didn't want to touch anything wanted four-hour on-site support.
We don't do this today.
We've really majored in learning how to do this over the last several months and I'm pleased to tell you that today we're ready to do this.
Now also for those customers that want to do this but they want to do it themselves so that they can take four hours to four seconds, we're providing them a spare parts kit so they can go in and make this easy change themselves.
So if you look at this list, seven things, we had to really hone on the last one, but we feel like we've got a great base to build upon here.
So again, when we step back from this, there was one thing among that list that they yelled louder than all the rest.
You know which one it was?
It was this one.
They're really sick of this.
They're almost sick to their stomachs of this.
And we feel like this better than that we can do this better than anyone else because we're one of the last companies that can provide the whole of the solution.
So today I'm very pleased to announce three separate offerings in this area, the premium service support plan, which is a three-year plan that includes hardware and software, the service parts kit that I referred to before, and professional services offerings where we will do a custom plan for our larger customers that want something unique.
And all of these are available today.
We anticipate the first two of those having an enormous attach rate to the servers that we sell.
So that's support.
Now I'd like to go to sales.
How do we sell it?
You may be wondering which target markets we might look at.
